His administration maintained a broadly prudent fiscal stance, implemented a 22% minimum-wage increase through Mexico's tripartite wage-setting body, and expanded transfers that measurably reduced recorded poverty and inequality. Labor poverty declined and formal employment recovered, although reopening, remittances, private hiring, and United States demand shared causation. Against those gains, fuel-price support was costly and poorly targeted, fiscal buffers remained depleted, and social-program incidence shifted away from some of the poorest households. The administration's state-favoring energy policy prompted unresolved treaty consultations and contributed to regulatory uncertainty, while health-access deprivation rose sharply and an independently evaluated priority health program had weak targeting and results design despite much larger funding. Banxico preserved monetary credibility, but largely through legally protected autonomy and despite presidential pressure, limiting personal credit. Trade claims, procurement indicators, and audit observations are allegations or risk signals rather than proven corruption or loss. The record therefore rejects a lower score dominated by instability or extraction, but weak implementation, uneven distribution, and limited durable capacity-building prevent a substantially higher
